subject: beetle
pitch: A proud stag beetle on a mossy log. A glossy chestnut wing case with a mirror shine, a black head and thorax, huge branched antler-like jaws in reddish brown, elbowed antennae with feathery tips, and six spiny black legs gripping the bark. A dewdrop clings to one of its antlers.
reasoning:
I don't have complete SDK documentation for every function signature, only a reference, so I need to be careful to stick to documented helpers like createBuilder, joint, chain, sweep, part, stick, surface, extrude, lathe, membrane, ring, and similar builder methods when designing this module.

I'm thinking through the stag beetle's scale—real specimens run roughly 3-7cm, so I'll model body length around 0.06m including antlers, with a mossy log scene piece about 0.3m long as the ground support. Since the whole model needs its lowest points touching y=0, I'll place the log on the floor and have the beetle's legs gripping the log's top surface, keeping the build simple with a root joint and basic part geometries to minimize errors.

I'm working out the log's placement as a cylinder along the Z-axis with radius 0.05m, rotated so its top sits around y=0.1, and deciding whether to use plain THREE.js meshes with custom bark/moss materials for scenery pieces versus the builder's part system, since scenery objects can be added directly to the root joint without needing the shared material constraints.

For the beetle itself, I'm sketching out the joint hierarchy—placing a root "body" joint around y=0.125 to match ground clearance above the log, then a child "head" joint slightly forward along Z. I'm uncertain how parent relationships are specified in the joint API, so I'm guessing it takes either a parent name or the returned joint object, and I'm planning to use chains for the antennae and mandibles with path arrays defining their shape.

For legs, I'm working out foot placement so they actually grip the log's curved surface: given the log radius and body height, I'm calculating the y-coordinate where the log's circular cross-section meets each foot's x-position, so the three pairs of legs land correctly on the bark rather than floating or sinking in.

I'm planning the elytra (wing case) as an ellipsoid scaled over the abdomen, picking colors for the chestnut shell, dark head, and mossy accents, and considering whether a part/scale approach can approximate the glossy beetle shell look.

Now I'm shaping the head and thorax as scaled spheres and ellipsoids, then building the stag mandibles as curved chains sweeping outward from the head with branching tines added via spikes at points along each chain, while figuring out how to attach hinge/jaw roles to the mandible joints.

For the dewdrop, I'm placing a small pale translucent-blue sphere at a tine tip, and I'm working out the elbowed antennae as a multi-point chain from scape to flagellum, planning a feathery club tip using a small ring of lamella-like spikes since texture-based card rendering isn't available.

For the along-path callback, I'm figuring out the correct signature so I can pass a frame into each part placement, then using it to scatter small ellipsoid plates along the antenna tip for the feathery look. Now I'm shifting to building the six legs as point chains with cone-shaped spines along each segment.

I'm working out precise foot, knee, and hip coordinates so each leg lands correctly on the log surface, varying the z-position per leg pair (front, mid, hind) to match the body segments they attach to. I'm sketching the chain-and-sweep approach for leg geometry, then adding spike-based spines along each leg using the along-path callback with a fixed upward direction.

I'm deciding to keep joint parenting simple by letting chains attach naturally to the root body joint rather than overthinking bone inheritance, and placing the mandibles off the head joint. For the log and moss, I'm treating them as static scenery parts attached to the root bone, using a cylinder geometry oriented along the body axis for the log, with moss blobs layered on top as simple sphere parts.

I'm working out the beetle's color scheme and body proportions, placing the elytra, thorax, and legs relative to the abdomen center, then designing the curved stag-beetle mandibles as a branching chain of points extending outward with small tine spikes.

I'm positioning the mandible spikes and tine tips, mirroring the left mandible geometry to generate the right side and matching antenna placement, then adding a small dewdrop sphere near the tine tip.

Placing the dewdrop on the tine tip, then sketching the head as a small sphere with subtle eye detail. For the mandible I'm chaining the base points and sweeping a tube along them, and for the antennae I'm laying out a jointed path with an elbow bend ending in a club, sweeping it thin, then scattering small lamella spheres along the club's tip using an along-path callback.

Now I'm working out the six legs, each as a four-point chain (hip, knee, ankle, foot) with front, mid, and hind pairs offset along the z-axis to vary stance, plus small spines scattered along each leg segment.

Next I'm designing the log the creature stands on: a bark-colored cylinder with patches of moss rendered as flattened spheres scattered around the top surface and ends, computing foot positions so they land correctly on the log's curved surface.

Then I'm moving on to the beetle itself, building the elytra as two mirrored halves, a black pronotum shield, and head, before setting up the body/head joint hierarchy and starting the actual build script with color constants for chestnut, black, jaw, bark, and moss tones.

Adding head details, eyes, and mandible geometry for the stag beetle...

Now I'm sketching out the tines with sweep-based geometry and a dewdrop detail at the tip, then building the antennae with a chained path and feathery lamellae plates along the club tip using the along-frame helper.

For the legs, I'm chaining hip-knee-ankle-foot points per side, sweeping them with a black material, and adding small cone-shaped spines along each leg using a frame-oriented part. I'm using a seeded random function to scatter moss blobs with varying scale and color around the log body, keeping everything above the floor, then wrapping up by defining a mirror helper for side-flipped points and returning the finished root structure.
